title: Quantitative Modelling of Solvation in 2D Materials via Alchemical Decoupling and Potential Energy Surfaces
authors: Lindsey N. Ioos, Duncan A. Peterson, Scott C. Warren
abstract: Understanding why 2D materials remain suspended in solutions is essential to understanding the mechanisms of aggregation and exfoliation. These dynamics have been difficult to model because of the long timescales and large activation energies involved in these simulations. Here we describe an improved strategy for modelling the solvation and stability of 2D materials that uses the Gibbs free energy of solvation to accurately calibrate two disconnected potential energy surfaces for the fully desolvated and fully solvated 2D materials. By joining these surfaces using solvation energy, we obtain predictions for 2D material stability in various solvents that are qualitatively different than prior simulations and that have excellent agreement with experimental results. Our approach predicts a much higher barrier to full desolvation of the material, suggesting that materials that appear to be aggregated in fact still retain monolayers of solvent between adjacent layers of 2D materials. This work provides much needed understanding on the interactions between the solvent and 2D material that can guide future experimental work.
summary: This paper develops an advanced simulation technique using alchemical decoupling to accurately model the solvation energy and stability of 2D materials like $	ext{MoS}_2$. By connecting separate potential energy surfaces, the authors predict that these materials resist full desolvation, maintaining a stable solvent layer between layers. This offers crucial insights into how solvents dictate the structural behavior and dispersion of 2D materials.
main_problem: The study aims to understand the solvation energy and stability of 2D materials, which is critical for predicting their aggregation and exfoliation mechanisms in solution.
main_result: The authors predict a significantly higher energy barrier for full desolvation compared to prior simulations, suggesting that 2D materials tend to retain a stable monolayer of solvent between layers.
method: They employ an improved simulation strategy using the Gibbs free energy of solvation ($\Delta G_{	ext{solv}}$) to connect two disconnected potential energy surfaces (PES) representing the fully desolvated and fully solvated states.
model_or_system: The system involves 2D materials, specifically $	ext{MoS}_2$, interacting with various solvents ($	ext{DMF}$, $	ext{DMSO}$, $	ext{IPA}$, $	ext{H}_2	ext{O}$). The modeling relies on calculating the solvation energy using alchemical decoupling.
key_observables: Gibbs free energy of solvation ($\Delta G_{	ext{solv}}$), Potential of Mean Force (PMF) curves, and areal density plots characterizing solvent structure.
important_parameters: Solvent types ($	ext{DMF}$, $	ext{DMSO}$, $	ext{IPA}$, $	ext{H}_2	ext{O}$), separation distances (e.g., $9.5 	ext{ Å}$ to $13.2 	ext{ Å}$), and the coupling parameter ($\lambda$) for alchemical decoupling.
main_assumptions: The method assumes that connecting the vacuum PES and solvent PES via $\Delta G_{	ext{solv}}$ correctly models the transition state, overcoming limitations of prior simulations that struggled with sheet bending.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the three-step method for calculating PMF curves, the setup for PMF simulations, and comparisons of calculated $\Delta G_{	ext{solv}}$ and molecule counts between sheets for different solvents.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the physical problem, details the advanced simulation methodology (alchemical decoupling to connect PES), presents quantitative results on solvation energies and structural stability across various solvents, and concludes by comparing findings with existing literature.
why_interesting: The work provides a rigorous, quantitative framework for calculating interfacial free energies in complex soft matter systems, which has implications for understanding interfaces in quantum materials and colloidal suspensions.
analysis_basis: full PDF text, analyzed in chunks

figures.caption: Fig. 1: Three step method for calculating PMF curves. (A) Step one involves calculating the energy of separating two sheets in a vacuum. (B) Once separated, the energy to solvate the sheets are calculated. (C) The sheets are then brought together while immersed in solvent. (D) This process calibrates the broken energy surfaces to create a full PMF curve.

Fig. 2: PMF simulation details. (A) The hexagonal MoS2 sheet used for simulations, 4.1 nm edge to edge length. (B) Sheets separated at maximum distance used in the simulation (25 Å) with solvent between. (C) Minimum distance between sheets (6.2Å), resulting in solvent ejected from the structure.

Fig. 3: The decoupling approach to calculating solvation energy. Beginning with all interactions turned off, LJ interactions are incrementally turned on. Once LJ interactions are fully turned on, the coulombic interactions are also incrementally turned on. The change in energy is calculated at each point, giving the total solvation energy.

Fig. 4: Results of the alchemical decoupling method for calculating solvation energy for simulations of DMF, DMSO, IPA, and H2O. (A) The LJ component is isolated and slowly turned on. (B) The coulombic component is then also turned on. (C) The total Gibbs free energy of solvation calculated.

Fig. 5: The changes in the number of molecules between the two sheets of MoS2 throughout the simulation are shown in (A) DMF, (B) DMSO, (C) IPA, and (D) H2O. The stable structures, visualized as plateaus in the areal density curve and the minima from the potential energy surfaces, are labelled and a snapshot of the simulation solvent orientation is pictured.
